title: The larger earthquake came first in 68% of selected shallow M5.8+ ComCat pairs in 2020-2025
abstract: We tested whether a published earthquake magnitude-order pattern also occurs in later years of a separate catalog. We used a fixed ComCat snapshot. Both events had magnitude at least 5.8 and depth below 70 km. Pairs had a magnitude gap of at least 0.5, a distance of at most 200 km, and a time gap from 1 to below 30 days. In 2020-2025, the larger event came first in 177 of 261 pairs, or 67.8%. The conditional 95% component-bootstrap interval was 54.8% to 77.9%. Equal weights for 43 connected groups gave 70.0%, with an interval of 57.8% to 81.7%. Removal of the largest group gave 65.4%. The 7-30 day check had an interval that included 50%. These results extend an earlier GCMT test beyond 2019. They do not identify causal links, prove a change between eras, or provide an earthquake forecast. Shared source methods, catalog errors, six test years and the component independence assumption limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, a figure and reproduction instructions are included. External records are not bundled.

display.caption: The larger-first fraction for selected shallow pairs. Left: pair weights and equal connected-group weights. Right: later-period checks. Bars show marginal 95% component-bootstrap intervals. The dashed line is equal order counts. Most checks overlap; they are not independent tests. The 7-30 day check does not exclude equal counts.

citations.reason: Source of the fixed pair-order question and cutoffs. Its GCMT sample ends in 2019. It already used component weights and omission checks. We write new code and test a later era in ComCat; this is not an independent replication in source methods.
Prior work on earthquake time asymmetry. It uses interevent-time increments, not our pair-magnitude score.
Triggering-cascade theory gives a possible account of foreshock and aftershock patterns. No causal model is fit here.
